Ireland's actual post-GRADUATION route is the 'Third Level Graduate Programme', which grants a Stamp 1G permission (generally 12 months for a Level 8 honours bachelor's degree, and a longer renewable initial permission for Level 9 or above) to non-EEA graduates of Irish institutions so they can seek graduate-level employment. I could not verify this from a primary source. The authoritative publisher, Immigration Service Delivery, is irishimmigration.ie, and that host was completely unreachable from this environment across six independent attempts and three different clients, so no page on it was ever fetched. Consequently I have NO fetched page containing the 12-month duration, the Level 8 / Level 9 distinction, the €300 registration fee, the six-month application window after being notified of the award, or the seven-year / eight-year aggregate student-pathway caps - and I will not write any of those numbers from memory. This is deliberately left UNAVAILABLE rather than backfilled from the search-engine snippets, which were summaries of an unread page and a 2017-revision policy PDF rather than text I retrieved. A corpus entry that filled this from memory would be unprovable.

sources.notes: Ireland has no route named 'permanent residence'. The end state for a non-EEA graduate on the Critical Skills path is CITIZENSHIP BY NATURALISATION after 5 years of legal residence - and that 5-year figure is confirmed verbatim on this page. The 5 years is counted as LEGAL RESIDENCE, not as years on a single visa, and it is reached well after the point at which the employment permit stops being needed (21 months), so a student should not model Ireland as '5 years on the work permit'. Corroborating figure from the gov.ie Department of Enterprise publication fetched in the same session, which expresses the same threshold in months: 'On achieving 60 months residency permission, Critical Skills Employment Permit or Green Card Employment Permit holders will then be permitted to make an application for long term residence'. Two independent official sources therefore agree on 5 years / 60 months, from different framings. Long-term residence (distinct from citizenship) is a separate status and the gov.ie text says the 60-month threshold permits an application for it; the distinct Irish 'long-term residence' scheme itself lives on irishimmigration.ie, which was unreachable, so its full criteria are NOT claimed here.

sources.notes: SOURCING CAVEAT, stated plainly: Ireland has no single government page like gov.uk's 'Money you need'. The financial-proof rule is split across the visa application criteria and the permission-to-stay registration criteria, and the page that would carry the underlying Department of Justice rules (irishimmigration.ie) was unreachable from this environment. This record therefore comes from citizensinformation.ie, the Citizens Information Board - a statutory public body of the Irish Government - rather than from the Department of Justice itself. It is an official public-body source, but it is a second-tier one for a legal requirement, and that is the correct degree of confidence to attach. THE TRAP, AND IT IS SHARPER THAN IN CANADA OR AUSTRALIA: the EUR 10,000 figure is stated as being required 'in addition to the course fees for each of those years', and course fees must separately be 'paid in full' as a separate bullet. So the EUR 10,000 is a living-cost threshold only; total funds needed for year one is EUR 10,000 PLUS the full first-year tuition PLUS private medical insurance. A budget built to EUR 10,000 alone is wrong by the entire tuition fee. The figure is ALSO time-scaled rather than flat: EUR 833 per month for courses giving a stay of 6 to 8 months (stated as EUR 4,998 for 6 months and EUR 6,665 for 8 months), rising to EUR 10,000 for a one-year course. Note that the page's own arithmetic is slightly loose - 833 x 6 = 4,998 and 833 x 8 = 6,664, but it prints 6,665 - so the monthly rate and the printed 8-month total do not agree exactly; I have recorded the printed figures verbatim rather than silently correcting them. The requirement applies to both visa-required and non-visa-required students, the latter proving it at the immigration desk on arrival rather than at a visa appointment. Course eligibility is restricted to full-time courses on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP) at NFQ level 6 or above, with a maximum 7 years of study at that level. NOT VERIFIED AND NOT CLAIMED, because they live only on the unreachable irishimmigration.ie page: the requirement that bank statements cover six months, the rejection of fixed-term savings accounts, the education-bond alternative worth a minimum of EUR 10,000 for degree students only, the instruction to pay at least EUR 6,000 of course fees before a visa application, and the Financial Summary Form. Those came from search-engine summaries of pages I did not retrieve, so they are excluded rather than asserted. Working-hours rights on the student stamp are recorded from this page since they materially affect whether a student can fund the gap above.

sources.notes: Ireland has no single national international tuition figure, so this is one named university: University College Dublin. The fee table is not in the parent page's HTML - it is loaded from the UCD Student Information System publish frame at https://sisweb.ucd.ie/usis/!W_HU_MENU.P_PUBLISH?p_tag=FEESLEVEL&RESD=NONEU&DGLEV=UG&ACYR=2026, which was fetched directly and from which the verbatim rows above are taken. An earlier webfetch of the parent page returned a variant prefatory line saying the EUR5 Students Union levy applied to students registered for the 2025-2026 academic year, whereas the browser-rendered parent page read on the same date says 2026-2027; the year of application is therefore recorded as 2026-27 from the later read and the discrepancy is flagged rather than silently reconciled. SPREAD IS THE HEADLINE POINT: across ordinary bachelor's degrees at UCD the 2026/27 non-EU rate runs from EUR 22,600 (BA, BSc Psychology, BSc Economics, BSc Social Sciences, Law, Music) through EUR 23,170 (Business/Commerce) and EUR 26,200 (BSc Sustainability) to EUR 29,500 (Computer Science, Science, Mathematics, Engineering, Physiotherapy, Nursing, Midwifery), then jumps sharply for professional programmes at EUR 36,250 (BSc Radiography), EUR 38,000 (Veterinary Medicine), EUR 44,880 (Graduate Entry Veterinary Medicine), EUR 63,890 (Medicine) and EUR 66,360 (Graduate Entry Medicine). A corpus that stored one Irish 'bachelor tuition' number would understate medicine by roughly three times. TOTALS ARE NOT SIMPLY MULTIPLY-UP: the page states fees are fixed at the entry-year level for programmes started from 2014/15 onward, EXCEPT Direct Entry Veterinary Medicine (DN300) and Graduate Entry Veterinary Medicine (DN301) which take annual increases - and its own footnote zv1 repeats this. Some programmes are also quoted per-year with different year values (BSc Radiography MDSJ: Year 1 32,880.00, Year 2 32,240.00, Year 3 16,120.00). Additional compulsory charges that a budget must carry and that are printed as footnotes: an additional Healthcare Screening charge of EUR330 for Medicine (zsa) and Physiotherapy (zsc), and an additional EUR2,000 in Year 2 for non-EU Psychology students (fb). Part-time study is priced per credit (Arts P/T BAU2: 376.70 per credit) and must not be annualised. Published figures include a Student Centre Levy but exclude the EUR5 Students Union levy. All amounts are in Euro as printed on the page.
